title: Kilmar Abrego Garcia can remain a free man for the holidays, judge rules
summary: A federal district judge ruled Monday that Kilmar Abrego Garcia can remain free from government custody, allowing him to spend the Christmas and New Year’s holidays with his family in Beltsville.
content:
by William J. Ford, Maryland Matters December 22, 2025

by William J. Ford, Maryland Matters December 22, 2025

A federal district judge ruled Monday that Kilmar Abrego Garcia can remain free from government custody, allowing him to spend the Christmas and New Year’s holidays with his family in Beltsville.

Judge Paula Xinis’ ruling came after a contentious one-hour hearing in U.S. District Court in Greenbelt during which she grilled Justice Department attorney Ernesto Molina, saying she was “growing beyond impatient” with the Trump administration’s constant “misrepresentations” in court.

Xinis kept a temporary restraining order in place to prohibit the Trump administration from detaining Abrego Garcia in the case she called “an extremely irregular and extraordinary situation.”

“Once again, I’m making a finding that these representations, which are misrepresentations, are in bad faith,” Xinis told Molina. “You cannot do that, OK? Judges take the rule of law very seriously and are faithful to giving both sides the opportunity to be heard.”

The case has shone a spotlight on the Trump administration’s aggressive immigration crackdown, since Abrego Garcia was detained in March by immigration officials and deported a harsh prison facility in his native El Salvador — despite a previous court ruling that prohibited his transfer there because of fear of violence by Salvadoran gangs.

Months after the U.S. Supreme Court’s April order that the Trump administration “facilitate” Abrego Garcia’s return, he was brought back to the U.S. on June 6, only to face charges of human smuggling three years ago in Tennessee. The judge in that case eventually ordered Abrego Garcia released to home detention while his claim of vindictive prosecution in the Tennessee case proceeded.

He returned home to Maryland, but a check-in with Immigration and Customs Enforcement, he was detained on immigration charges and held ain a Pennsylvania jail.

Xinis, who became involved in the case when Abrego Garcia was first deported, ordered the Trump administration on Dec. 11 to release him from the Moshannon Valley Processing Center in Pennsylvania, where he had been held since September. She wrote in the order then that the Trump administration was “again without lawful authority” for holding Abrego Garica for deportation, without making an effort to remove him to a third country.

Costa Rica has agreed to accept Abrego Garcia as a refugee, but Justice Department lawyers could not give Xinis a clear explanation of why the Trump administration would not send him there. Instead, the administration has proposed deporting Abrego Garcia to various countries in Africa.

When Abrego Garcia did a check-in at the ICE field office in Baltimore on Dec. 12, he was not detained but walked out about an hour later to leave and spend time with family in Prince George’s County.

On Monday, Abrego Garica arrived at the courthouse in Greenbelt around 12:30 p.m. for a 1 p.m. hearing, his first court appearance before Xinis since the case began with his detention in March. Xinis began the hearing with a slight joke about the six lawyers representing Abrego Garcia at the hearing.

“Mr. Abrego Garcia, you almost have a baseball team representing you today,” Xinis said.

Abrego Garcia quietly sat the table during the slightly more than one-hour hearing and only said, “Good afternoon your honor, my name is Kilmar Abrego Garcia.”

In regards to her earlier order, Xinis on Monday asked Molina who signed a memorandum that her order was issued on “ex parte” basis, meaning one side was not heard or notified.

“I don’t know who the author of that would be because that would be incorrect,” Molina said.

“Wrong,” the judge interjected. “Everybody signed it, and it’s flat wrong. So who did that? There’s like four lawyers that signed this. I want to know who.”

Molina didn’t say who wrote the memorandum, but conceded it was wrong.

“So in the future, I’ll say it again, [be] really careful what you write and make sure it’s factually accurate,” Xinis said.

About 100 supporters rallied for Abrego Garcia outside the courthouse Monday, singing songs and coordinating various chants.

After the hearing, one of Abrego Garcia’s attorneys, Simon Y. Sandoval-Moshenberg, said his client was ready to go to Costa Rica today.

“It’s actually the federal government that’s keeping him here in the United States right now,” he said. “Again, they’re insisting on punishing him and using ICE detention … to keep him locked up. We’re not going to allow that. We’re going to keep fighting against it.”

But in the meantime, the judge ordered the government’s attorneys to respond by Friday on how they plan to handle Abrego Garcia’s immigration case. His attorneys have until Dec. 30 to file their response to the government.

“The judge will decide whether to convert her temporary order prohibiting his rearrest into a permanent order, or whether to dissolve it,” Sandoval-Moshenberg said. “As of right now, Mr. Abrego Garcia is going to return to his home with his wife and his children, his family members in Maryland, and he will be back home through Christmas and New Year.”
